---
title: "Embedding"
description: "Using a method's array surface inside a forecasting library that already owns its cross-validation loop."
---

Most of this site is written for people who want a calibrated interval out of a
forecaster. This page is for the other audience: maintainers of a forecasting
library who want conformal calibration *inside* it, without taking on
`conformalforecast`'s orchestration or its view of the world.

That is what the **array surface** is for: `method.fit` on numpy arrays returns
a fitted object, whose `interval` (and, for online methods, `update`) you call
from then on. It takes no forecaster, no adapter and no DataFrame.

## The invariant

> An array-surface signature may only accept numpy-coercible arrays and
> plain-Python config — never adapters, DataFrames, or library types.

This holds across `methods/`, `nonconformity/` and `panel.py`, and it is the
entire reason those modules are embeddable. A method has no opinion about how
you produce forecasts, where your data lives, or what your cross-validation
looks like. It takes arrays and gives back arrays.

```python
import numpy as np
from conformalforecast import SplitConformal

# predictions/truths: (n_series, n_windows, horizon)
method = SplitConformal(alpha=0.1)
fitted = method.fit(predictions, truths)
interval = fitted.interval(new_predictions)   # (n_series, n_samples, horizon, 2)
```

Keep the **returned** object: `fit` never modifies `method`, so the method is a
reusable, serializable description of the calibration (`method.model_dump()`)
and `fitted` is the per-model state your library stores next to the model it
calibrates. For an online method, `fitted.update(prediction, truth)` advances
that state in place; `fitted.model_copy(deep=True)` takes a snapshot.

Construction is keyword-only (`SplitConformal(alpha=0.1)`) because every method
is a pydantic model, and an out-of-range `alpha` is a `pydantic.ValidationError`
rather than a bare `ValueError` — worth knowing if you re-raise it as your own
error type. The nonconformity score is config too:
`SplitConformal(alpha=0.1, score=AbsoluteResidual())`, rejected at construction
if the method cannot invert it. `fit` works on a copy of it, retained on the
fitted object as `score_fn_` for `interval` to invert with.

Nothing here needs an adapter. An object fitted through the array surface alone
has no `forecaster_`, so its `predict` raises `CalibrationError` pointing you at
`interval` — the two surfaces do not have to be mixed, and for an embedding they
should not be.

The dependency you take on is narwhals, numpy, pydantic and scipy — nothing else. Importing
`conformalforecast` never imports statsforecast, mlforecast, neuralforecast or
torch.

## What you get that a hand-rolled quantile does not

A library that already computes `np.quantile` on its residuals is most of the
way there. What the array surface adds is the parts that are easy to get subtly
wrong:

- **The exact conformal quantile.** Split and CQR take
  `k = ceil((1 - alpha)(n + 1))` as an order statistic, not an interpolated
  quantile. The `n + 1` is what makes the coverage guarantee finite-sample. The
  adaptive methods need a time-varying level, so ACI and AgACI use a linear
  quantile and NexCP and WeightedSplit a weighted one.
- **Version-stable arithmetic.** `_quantiles.py` computes its interpolation
  constant in `float64` regardless of input dtype. numpy changed that behaviour
  in 2.5; following numpy would have shifted every `float32` interval bound on an
  upgrade. Output is identical across numpy versions by contract, with tests
  pinning it.
- **NaN-aware ragged handling.** Per-series effective counts, masked order
  statistics, and `InsufficientCalibrationSamples` naming the series that are too
  short. See [ragged panels](../capabilities/ragged-panels).
- **`float32` preservation.** No silent upcast of neural network output.
- **Batched math.** Nothing loops over the `(n_series × horizon)` grid in
  Python. The per-cell quantile is one gather, and the online methods keep an
  incrementally-sorted history rather than re-quantiling from scratch each step.
  SPCI, which fits one regressor per cell, is the sanctioned exception.
- **Five more methods.** Once the array contract is satisfied, [ACI](../methods/aci),
  [AgACI](../methods/agaci), [NexCP](../methods/nexcp), [CQR](../methods/cqr) and
  [SPCI](../methods/spci) are the same three calls — `fit`, `interval`, and
  `update` for the online four. CQR's `fit` and `interval` take a quantile cube
  rather than point forecasts, with a trailing `(q_lo, q_hi)` axis.

## The reference migration

`conformalforecast.compat.mlforecast_shim` is a worked example of embedding a
method behind an existing library's interval hook — mlforecast's
`_INTERVAL_METHODS` registry.

```python
from conformalforecast.compat.mlforecast_shim import register_interval_method
from conformalforecast import SplitConformal

register_interval_method("conformal_method_split", SplitConformal)
```

`register_interval_method` takes the method *class* plus any extra config
keywords (`gamma=`, `rho=`, `seed=`) and constructs one method per requested
level, since `alpha` comes from the level. It is deliberately a *shim*, not a
supported API: the expectation is that the upstream PR copies the pattern
in-repo and this module is deleted. Read its module docstring before writing
your own — it documents the three things that turned out to be fiddly, all of
which will apply to any library:

**Array layout.** mlforecast's conformity scores arrive window-major,
`(cs_n_windows, n_series, cs_h)`, and the array surface wants
`(n_series, n_windows, horizon)`. One transpose. Note that the shim does *not*
use `panel.long_to_panel` for this — the scores are already a contiguous cube,
and pivoting would re-sort the series axis away from mlforecast's own order.
Getting the series axis to line up with the caller's is the single most common
integration bug.

**Score reconstruction.** mlforecast drops the target column before the hook
runs, so its `cs_df` holds `abs(prediction - truth)` and the signed residual is
unrecoverable. The shim reconstructs the method's input as `predictions = 0`,
`truths = scores` — exact under `AbsoluteResidual`, and wrong under any signed or
quantile score. It therefore *rejects* methods whose default score is anything
else, rather than producing a plausible wrong number. If your library can
preserve the sign, do; it unlocks the signed-score methods.

**A stricter calibration floor.** `fit` requires `ceil(1/alpha)` effective
windows per series and raises otherwise. mlforecast's native methods interpolate
a quantile from as few as two. This will look like a regression to your users and
is not one — it is the sample size the requested quantile actually needs — so
surface the error rather than papering over it.

## Two upstream changes the shim wants

Both are small, and both are documented in the module docstring:

1. `PredictionIntervals.__init__` validates `method` against a hard-coded list
   rather than `_INTERVAL_METHODS.keys()`, so a newly registered name is
   reachable through `get_conformal_method` but not through
   `PredictionIntervals(method=...)`. One line.
2. `compute_conformity_scores` already takes `signed=`, but `MLForecast.fit`
   never passes `signed=True` on the ordinary path. Threading it through would
   make the signed-score methods usable.

## Not supported by the shim

`weights` / `target_weights` (density-ratio reweighting) and `is_transfer=True`
(pooled cross-domain calibration) raise `NotImplementedError`. NexCP's `rho`
decay is a *different* mechanism and must not be silently substituted for
density-ratio weights — they answer different questions and would give different
intervals under the same name.
